title: Placebo effect in the rat.
abstract: Scopolamine hydrobromide disrupts the learned behavior of rats in a predictable manner. Physiological saline mimics to some extent the effect of the drug when the two substances are alternately administered in a series of injections. This placebo effect appears to be an instance of simple Pavlovian conditioning.

screening.rationale: Empirical animal experiment that tested and reported a placebo-like (saline) effect produced by Pavlovian conditioning versus an active drug (scopolamine).

classification.summary: Found that saline injections came to mimic scopolamine's disruption of learned rat behavior, consistent with Pavlovian conditioning producing a placebo-like effect.
classification.key_finding: Saline administered alternately with scopolamine produced behavioral disruption similar to the drug, interpreted as conditioned placebo effect.

title: Controlled trials: nuisance or necessity?
abstract: Placebos can mimic in many ways the characteristics of active drugs. The importance of placebo controls in clinical trials in the evaluation of therapeutic efficacy and side action liability of drugs is exemplified by specific examples from human experimentation. It is concluded that controlled trials will prevent many of the errors inherent in uncontrolled therapeutic observations.

screening.rationale: Methodological journal article whose primary focus was the role and importance of placebo controls in clinical trials (placebo science/methodology).

classification.summary: Argued for the necessity of placebo controls in clinical trials, illustrating with human examples how placebos prevent errors inherent in uncontrolled therapeutic observations.
